chunks.text:
A hash table stores key-value pairs so that looking up a key takes constant time on average. It keeps an array of slots, often called buckets. To store a pair, the table runs the key through a hash function, which turns the key into an integer, and then takes that integer modulo the array length to pick a bucket. Looking a key up repeats the same steps, so the table jumps straight to the right bucket instead of scanning every entry the way a list would.

A good hash function has three properties. It is deterministic: the same key always gives the same hash, otherwise a stored value could never be found again. It is fast to compute, because it runs on every insert and every lookup. And it spreads keys evenly across the buckets, so that no bucket ends up holding far more than its share. A poor hash, for example one that only looks at the first letter of a string, sends many keys to the same few buckets and the table slows down.

Because keys are hashed, a hash table does not keep them in any useful order. If you need the keys sorted, or you need range queries such as all keys between 10 and 20, a balanced search tree is usually the better structure. Keys must also be immutable while they are stored: if a key changes after insertion, its hash changes, and the table will look for it in the wrong bucket.
key_points: A hash table gives average constant-time lookup by mapping each key to a bucket in an array.
The bucket index is the key's hash taken modulo the array length.
A good hash function is deterministic, fast, and spreads keys evenly across buckets.
Hash tables keep no key order, and stored keys must not change after insertion.

chunks.text:
Two different keys can land in the same bucket. This is called a collision, and it is unavoidable: there are far more possible keys than buckets. A hash table needs a rule for handling collisions, and there are two common families.

Separate chaining stores a small list in each bucket. A new pair that collides is simply appended to that bucket's list, and a lookup hashes to the bucket and then walks its short list comparing keys. Chaining is simple and degrades gracefully: a slightly crowded table just has slightly longer lists.

Open addressing keeps every entry directly in the array. When the chosen slot is taken, the table probes other slots in a fixed sequence until it finds a free one. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the one after, and so on. It is cache-friendly because it reads neighbouring memory, but it suffers from primary clustering: occupied slots bunch together into long runs, and every key that hashes into a run has to walk to its end. Quadratic probing and double hashing jump further away on each step, which breaks up those runs.

Deletion is tricky with open addressing. If you simply empty a slot, a later lookup can stop at the gap and wrongly conclude that a key further along the probe sequence is missing. Tables therefore mark deleted slots with a special tombstone value that lookups skip over but inserts may reuse.
key_points: A collision is when two keys map to the same bucket, and it cannot be avoided.
Separate chaining keeps a list per bucket and appends colliding pairs to it.
Open addressing probes other slots; linear probing is cache-friendly but causes primary clustering.
Deleting under open addressing needs tombstones so lookups do not stop early.

chunks.text:
The load factor of a hash table is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It is the main dial for performance. With chaining, the average list length equals the load factor, so lookups stay fast while it is small. With open addressing the effect is sharper: as the load factor approaches 1, free slots become rare and probe sequences grow very long.

To keep the load factor low, a table resizes when it passes a threshold, commonly around 0.75 for chaining and lower, around 0.5, for open addressing. Resizing allocates a larger array, usually double the size, and rehashes every entry, because each key's bucket depends on the array length. A single resize costs O(n) time, but because the array doubles, resizes become rarer as the table grows. Spread over all the inserts, the cost per insert is still constant on average. This is called amortised O(1).

The constant-time promise is an average, not a guarantee. If many keys hash to the same bucket, either by bad luck, a weak hash function, or an attacker choosing keys on purpose, lookups degrade to O(n). Some languages defend against this by seeding their string hash with a random value at start-up, and Java's HashMap turns very long bucket chains into balanced trees so the worst case becomes O(log n).
key_points: Load factor is entries divided by buckets, and it controls how fast lookups are.
Tables resize past a threshold by allocating a bigger array and rehashing every entry.
Doubling on resize makes the cost per insert amortised O(1) even though one resize is O(n).
Average O(1) is not guaranteed; many keys in one bucket degrade lookups to O(n).
